passages.t: ‘There is but a step between me and death’
passages.happening:
David flees from Ramah and comes to Jonathan. “What have I done? What is my iniquity? How have I sinned against your father, that he wants to take my life?” (verse 1).

Jonathan cannot believe it. His father does nothing without telling him, he says (verse 2). But David answers that Saul knows how close they are and is keeping it from Jonathan. ‘As surely as the LORD lives and as you yourself live, there is but a step between me and death’ (verse 3). Jonathan answers, “Whatever you desire, I will do for you” (verse 4).

David proposes a test. Tomorrow is the New Moon, when he should eat at the king's table. He will hide in the field instead. If Saul misses him, Jonathan is to say that David asked to go to Bethlehem for his clan's yearly sacrifice (verses 5-6). If Saul says good, David is safe. If he is enraged, Jonathan will know he means harm (verse 7).

David appeals to their covenant: ‘for you have brought me into a covenant with you before the LORD’ (verse 8). If he is guilty, Jonathan should kill him himself. “Never!” Jonathan replied (verse 9). They go out together into the field (verse 11).
passages.hearers:
This is the last time David and Jonathan are together at Saul's court. After it David never returns there. The chapter settles whether he can make peace with Saul, and the answer is no.

The New Moon, the first day of each month in Israel's calendar, was a holy day with special offerings and the blowing of trumpets. At Saul's court it meant a feast of at least two days. Clans also held their own yearly sacrifices, often at local places of worship, before the temple in Jerusalem became the one central sanctuary. So David's excuse was believable.

Jonathan's disbelief is honest. He loves his father and thinks he knows him. David is the one who has seen the spear.
passages.later:
Proverbs knows this kind of friend: ‘there is a friend who stays closer than a brother’ (Proverbs 18:24).

The law set the New Moon among Israel's holy days: ‘and the beginning of each month, you are to blow the trumpets over your burnt offerings and fellowship offerings’ (Numbers 10:10).
passages.hard:
David proposes a cover story for Jonathan to tell Saul. Does the Bible approve of it?

The plan depends on an excuse, and the text never says whether David actually went to Bethlehem. Readers answer in different ways. Some argue that the excuse may have been true, or that it was a fair way to test a king who had already tried to murder David and had broken a sworn oath (19:6). Others hold that it was a real deception, and that the Bible, as it often does, simply reports it without approval, so that readers see a faith that was real but not flawless. David will use deception again in chapter 21, with serious consequences.

The chapter's attention is elsewhere, on the covenant between the two friends and on what Saul really intends. It neither holds up David's cover story as a model nor condemns it outright.
passages.asks: David said there was but a step between him and death, and his friend said, ‘Whatever you desire, I will do for you.’ Ask who would say that to you, and to whom you would say it. And ask whether you have ever refused to believe a hard truth about someone you love.

passages.happening:
In the field Jonathan swears by the LORD that he will find out his father's mind and tell David, and send him away safely if Saul means him harm (verses 12-13). ‘May the LORD be with you, just as He has been with my father’ (verse 13).

Then he asks something for himself. “And as long as I live, treat me with the LORD’s loving devotion, that I may not die” (verse 14). And he asks David never to cut off his loving devotion from his household, even when the LORD cuts off all David's enemies (verse 15).

So Jonathan makes a covenant with the house of David (verse 16). ‘And Jonathan had David reaffirm his vow out of love for him, for Jonathan loved David as he loved himself’ (verse 17).

Then he lays out the plan. David is to hide by the stone Ezel. Jonathan will shoot three arrows and send a boy to find them. If he tells the boy the arrows are on this side, David is safe. If he says they are beyond him, David must go, ‘for the LORD has sent you away’ (verses 18-22). ‘And as for the matter you and I have discussed, the LORD is a witness between you and me forever’ (verse 23).
passages.hearers:
Jonathan says openly that the LORD will cut off David's enemies. He knows what that means for himself. As long as David lives, Jonathan will not be king. He submits to God's purpose instead of fighting it, while his father fights the same purpose with a spear.

Loving devotion, chesed in Hebrew, is loyalty that goes beyond what is owed, the faithfulness that keeps a promise when it would be easier to let it go. Jonathan asks for ‘the LORD’s loving devotion’, asking David to treat his family the way God treats his people.

In the ancient world a new royal house often wiped out the family of the old one. So Jonathan's request was far from a formality. He is asking for the lives of his children.

The covenant is sworn in the LORD's name, which makes God its witness. The chapter is framed by oaths by the LORD, at the start and at the end, so the friendship is set in God's presence.

The arrows let Jonathan warn David without being seen talking to him. A boy running after an archer's arrows was an ordinary sight.
passages.later:
Proverbs says of such a friend, ‘A friend loves at all times, and a brother is born for adversity’ (Proverbs 17:17).

David kept this covenant as king. He told Jonathan's son, ‘surely I will show you kindness for the sake of your father Jonathan’ (2 Samuel 9:7). And when the lives of Saul's descendants were demanded, ‘the king spared Mephibosheth son of Jonathan, the son of Saul, because of the oath before the LORD between David and Jonathan son of Saul’ (2 Samuel 21:7).
passages.asks: Jonathan asked David to keep faith with his children after he was gone. Ask what promises you have made that will outlast you, and whether you are keeping them. And ask what it would cost you to welcome God's purpose when it means someone else rises and you do not.

passages.t: An empty seat, and a spear thrown at a son
passages.happening:
David hides in the field. At the New Moon feast Saul sits in his usual place by the wall, with Jonathan opposite and Abner beside him, ‘but David’s place was empty’ (verse 25). The first day Saul says nothing. He thinks David must be ceremonially unclean (verse 26).

On the second day the seat is still empty, and Saul asks Jonathan, “Why hasn’t the son of Jesse come to the meal either yesterday or today?” (verse 27). Jonathan gives the agreed answer: David asked to go to Bethlehem for his clan's sacrifice (verses 28-29).

Saul's anger blazes. He insults Jonathan and his mother, and he says plainly what he fears: “For as long as the son of Jesse lives on this earth, neither you nor your kingship shall be established. Now send for him and bring him to me, for he must surely die!” (verse 31).

“Why must he be put to death?” Jonathan replied. “What has he done?” (verse 32). Saul hurls his spear at Jonathan to kill him. ‘So Jonathan knew that his father was determined to kill David’ (verse 33). Jonathan leaves the table in fierce anger and eats nothing, grieved at his father's shameful treatment of David (verse 34).
passages.hearers:
The seating gives a glimpse of a small court: the king by the wall, Jonathan opposite, Abner the commander, Saul's cousin, beside him, and a place kept for David. In so small a circle an empty seat was noticed at once.

Because the feast was tied to a sacrifice, someone who was ritually unclean could not take part, for instance after touching a dead body. That is why Saul first assumes David is unclean. Being unclean was not the same as sin. It was a passing state that kept a person from holy things until washing and waiting made them clean again.

Saul's insult attacks Jonathan's mother in order to shame the son, a way of calling him disloyal by birth. Then he speaks the hard political fact: as long as David lives, Jonathan will never be king. Saul is fighting for a throne God has already taken from him.

Jonathan answers with two questions, the same ones David asked him. What has he done? The answer is a spear.
passages.later: The law gives the reason Saul assumed David had stayed away: ‘But if anyone who is unclean eats meat from the peace offering that belongs to the LORD, that person must be cut off from his people’ (Leviticus 7:20).
passages.hard:
A father hurls a spear at his own son. What does the chapter make of a father's rage?

The chapter shows a family torn apart by a father's jealousy. Jonathan has to choose between loyalty to his father and loyalty to what is right. He chooses what is right at great cost to himself, while still honoring his father as far as he can. He does not strike back. He leaves the table, grieving, and goes to warn his friend.

The text does not call Saul's rage anything but what it is. Saul's anger has become stronger than his love for his own son.

Nothing in this passage asks anyone to stay where they or their children are in danger. If you are being hurt, at home, at work or in a church, tell someone you trust and get help. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: Jonathan honored his father as far as he could, and would not join his father's wrong. Ask where loyalty to someone you love is asking you to share in their wrong. And ask how you can refuse it without hatred.

passages.t: Arrows in the field, and a parting
passages.happening:
In the morning Jonathan goes out to the field with a small boy. “Run and find the arrows I shoot” (verse 36). He shoots an arrow beyond the boy and calls out, “Isn’t the arrow beyond you?” (verse 37). “Hurry! Make haste! Do not delay!” (verse 38). The boy gathers the arrows, knowing nothing. Only Jonathan and David know what the signal means (verse 39). Jonathan sends the boy back to the town with his weapons (verse 40).

When the boy is gone, David comes out from beside the stone and bows to the ground three times. ‘Then he and Jonathan kissed each other and wept together’ (verse 41), David weeping more.

Jonathan says, ‘Go in peace, for the two of us have sworn in the name of the LORD’ (verse 42). They have sworn that the LORD will be a witness between them and between their children forever. David goes his way, and Jonathan goes back into the town.
passages.hearers:
The plan is carried out exactly as it was laid out. Jonathan's words to the boy are also words to David, hidden in the field: the arrow is beyond you, hurry, do not delay. The LORD has sent him away.

The last scene is spare. Two friends kiss and weep. The narrator's small note that David wept more says a great deal in a few words. He is leaving his friend, his wife, his place at court and his home, and he does not know when he will be safe again.

Jonathan sends him away in peace. The Hebrew word shalom means wholeness and safety, not only the absence of war, and here it is spoken in the middle of danger.

They will meet once more, briefly, in the wilderness (23:16-18). After that, the next word David hears of Jonathan will be of his death.
passages.later: Chronicles records how the friendship ended: ‘they killed Saul’s sons Jonathan, Abinadab, and Malchishua’ (1 Chronicles 10:2). When the news came of Jonathan's death on Mount Gilboa, David sang, “How the mighty have fallen in the thick of battle! Jonathan lies slain on your heights” (2 Samuel 1:25).
passages.asks: David and Jonathan parted in tears, trusting the LORD to keep what they had sworn. Ask who you have had to part from, and whether you can entrust that bond to God. And ask whether you have told the people you love what they mean to you before a parting comes.
